html:
Nigiri sushi, a slice of fresh fish pressed onto a small mound of vinegared rice, appeared in Edo (Tokyo) in the 1820s. The cook Hanaya Yohei is usually credited with it.

Older sushi was a way to keep fish: it was packed in rice and left to ferment for months. Later, cooks added vinegar to the rice to speed things up and pressed fish and rice in boxes. Nigiri was faster still. Made on the spot with fish from Edo Bay, it was sold from street stalls as quick food for busy townspeople in the biggest city in the world, which had passed a million people a century before.

The style was called Edomae, "in front of Edo", after the bay. Fish was often lightly cured, marinated or simmered, since there was no ice.

After the Great Kantō earthquake of 1923, many Tokyo sushi makers moved elsewhere in Japan and spread the style. In the later 1900s nigiri spread around the world, along with other Japanese foods such as ramen.
